<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
The re-analysis is valuable. Its four specific findings largely hold, and it confirms with microdata several problems that could only be inferred from the Halden working paper. But the Comment makes the same kind of error it criticises, in the opposite direction. Halden turned a modest, uncertain result into "sector-general" gains. This Comment turns a residual ~11% gain, which matches the randomised evidence, into "entirely an artifact". The evidence supports neither.

## What holds up

The arithmetic checks:

| Quantity | Check |
|---|---|
| Hours ratio, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 ✓ (−14.1%) |
| Hours ratio, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 ✓ (−13.9%) |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 → +18.9% ✓ |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 → +14.6% ✓ |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 → +10.8% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 → −2.6% ✓ |
| "Roughly four points" (output) | ✓ |
| "Roughly six points" (hours) | 20 − 14.1 ✓ |

Several findings are useful:

- **Attrition.** This is the most important finding. Seven of the nine withdrawals came *after* the schedule began, and most gave output-related reasons. That contradicts the working paper's account. If it's accurate, Halden's description needs correcting.
- **Manager overstatement.** The manager index exceeded the record-based index in 19 of 23 organisations (sign test p ≈ 0.003). That is a systematic pattern.
- **Subset representativeness.** The manager-reported means in the subsets (98.9 and 98.4) are close to the full-sample 98.7. That gives some reassurance the subsets aren't wildly unrepresentative, at least on that measure. The Comment could say so.
- **Data note and recommendations.** The data note is candid, and the recommendations are sound.

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the paper's own results

- After every correction the authors could make, a gain of **+10.8%** in output per actual hour remains.
- The step from there to "entirely an artifact" rests on two unquantified arguments: that attrition removed the worst performers (not corrected for in Table 2), and that the residual is a novelty effect (not tested).
- Section 6 concedes that "six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one." If that can't be distinguished, the evidence can't support the claim that the gain is *entirely* novelty.
- The data note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the conclusion generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.

## 2. The Varden evidence is used selectively

- The Comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It then leaves out Varden's *other* registered primary result: in case-processing offices, output per actual hour rose **+12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4)**.
- That design used record-based output, timesheet hours and randomisation, which removes exactly the measurement and selection problems this Comment identifies.
- The Comment's own corrected Halden figure (+10.8%) is close to that, from a completely different design. Two independent estimates using records and actual hours converge on roughly 11–12% in non-coverage work, over six to nine months. That points against "entirely an artifact".
- Varden's gain persisted at nine months. That is already beyond the Comment's own extrapolated novelty fade (see section 3 below), though it doesn't settle durability.

## 3. The novelty argument is the weakest part, and the Comment didn't test it with data it had

**It projects a trend from two data points.**
- Energy readings of 0.61 SD at month 3 and 0.29 SD at month 6 give a linear decline of about 0.107 SD per month.
- On that line, energy would reach zero at about month **8.7**, not "around month ten". That is a minor arithmetic point.
- The bigger issue is that two points can't distinguish linear decay from a plateau.

**It measures the wrong thing.** Self-reported energy isn't output. The argument needs output to decline over time, not enthusiasm.

**The direct test was available.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*, and the authors have the microdata. If the gain were novelty, output per hour should fall from early to late months. The Comment never examines this, even though it is the obvious test of its central claim.

**The burden-of-proof framing is inconsistent.** It is fair to say durability is unproven. It doesn't follow that the gain is therefore known to be absent, which is what the conclusion claims.

## 4. The critique of the meetings hypothesis is partly inaccurate, and applies a double standard

**It misdescribes the Varden analysis.**
- The meeting data were collected in month six, before the nine-month results existed. That makes "selected for analysis after the results were known" misleading.
- The seven offices are the *entire* treated case-processing stratum, not a chosen subgroup.
- Varden didn't claim a mechanism. They wrote that the correlation "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test.

**Halden supports the hypothesis independently.** Halden's interviews (47 of 58 managers reporting fewer meetings) come from a different setting and point the same way.

**The standards are uneven.** The Comment rejects a caveated correlation across seven offices as post hoc. Yet it offers its own novelty explanation based on two readings of a self-reported scale, with no output test. The meetings account is also a direct rival to the novelty account for the residual gain. If it's correct, the gain is plausibly durable. The Comment should treat both as open hypotheses.

## 5. The abstract misstates the analysis

- **The corrections listed don't match Table 2.** The abstract says "Correcting the first three, the gain … falls … to 10.8%." The first three problems listed are attrition, output measure and hours, but Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described, never corrected.
- **"Four problems account for most of the reported gain."** The revenue problem has no bearing on the per-hour gain. And the corrections that were made reduce it by about 54% (23.4 → 10.8). "About half" is more accurate than "most".

## 6. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

Section 3 attributes the gap between 20% and 14.1% to longer days (+0.7 hours per day) and logged day-off work (1.6 hours per week). Reconstructing pilot-period hours from those components:

- From the 32 scheduled hours: 32 + 4 × 0.7 + 1.6 = **36.4 hours**.
- From the baseline daily average (40.3 / 5 = 8.06 h): 4 × 8.76 + 1.6 ≈ **36.6 hours**.

Both are well above the reported **34.6**. Either the components are mis-stated or something else reduced hours (leave, absence, part-weeks). The difference matters:

- If actual hours were about 36.5, the hours reduction was only about 9.5%.
- That would leave the per-hour gain even smaller than 10.8%.

Either way, the authors should reconcile the figures.

## 7. Attrition should be quantified, not just described

The Comment shows that attrition was non-random but doesn't estimate how much it matters. The microdata allow bounding:

- Assign the nine withdrawals a gain of zero, or a pessimistic output figure, and recompute on an intention-to-treat basis.
- Or use Lee-style bounds.

Without that, "attrition removed the organisations least able to cope" can't be counted towards the "entirely an artifact" conclusion.

## 8. The record-based output measure has its own problems

- **Billable hours.** "Billable hours delivered" is one of the record types used. As an output measure in an hours-reduction study, it is close to circular: output per hour then becomes a utilisation rate. The Comment should say how many of the 23 used it, and show results without them.
- **Gameable counts.** Tickets closed and cases completed can be shifted by changes in case mix, as with Varden's case-processing offices.
- **Undisclosed method.** The method for computing the "implied" index isn't described: baseline period, seasonal adjustment, how mixed record types were combined.

The direction of the manager bias is credible. The exact 3.8-point figure is less certain than presented.

## 9. Smaller points

- **Deflator.** CPI isn't the right deflator for organisations' revenue. Sector output price indices would be better. The real-terms point probably survives, but "approximately 2.6%" is more precise than CPI justifies.
- **Retail sample size.** The retail figure from records (−11.2%) rests on three organisations. It should be labelled as such, especially since it is presented alongside the Varden result as corroboration.
- **Varden's limits.** Varden's counter result is randomised but rests on five offices per arm. "The most reliable finding in the literature" is defensible. The Comment's uncritical reliance on it contrasts with how it treats Varden's other results.

## Overall

**The evidence supports:**
- Halden's headline 23.4% roughly halves under the corrections that are possible: about +11% in output per actual hour, in a non-random subset of survivors.
- Attrition probably biases even that upwards, by an unquantified amount.
- In coverage-bound work, output per employee falls.
- Durability beyond six to nine months is unknown.

**It does not support:**
- That per-hour gains are "entirely" an artifact. The residual matches the one randomised estimate in non-coverage work.
- That novelty explains the residual. This is untested, and the monthly output data that could test it went unused.

The paper's sections 1–5 make a strong comment. Sections 6–8 should be rewritten to:
1. Bound the attrition effect.
2. Test output trajectories month by month.
3. Engage with Varden's case-processing result.
4. Treat novelty and meeting reduction as competing open hypotheses.

A defensible conclusion would be something like: *"The reported gain is overstated by roughly half. The remainder is consistent with randomised evidence from non-coverage work, but its durability is unestablished."*

There's also a broader pattern across this set of documents. Halden overclaimed, Varden calibrated, and this Comment corrects the overclaim and then overcorrects. It's the "failures come in pairs" point from the first document, applied correctly this time.
